rv.q: In short, these are ridiculous figures — and yet not so ridiculous as to be unrecognizable.
FastHorse effectively roasts her characters as turkeys, trussed by their own self-consciousness.
For all its knife-sharp humor, the play might be compared to a delicious Thanksgiving meal that nevertheless makes you feel a bit overstuffed, and slightly tired of your family, too.
But the objects of its satire seem both too easy a mark and already expired.

The production problems evident here are rooted in a lack of believability: FastHorse’s premise only works if you can imagine this little crew really existing and the actors and director have to make that happen.

FastHorse’s attempt to have her characters bounce between extreme political correctness and overt ignorance results in a muddled theatrical experience that is not quite hilarious, not quite provocative and not quite informative, but has the aftertaste of all three.

The problem is that The Thanksgiving Play intentionally hurtles its characters toward a dead end — like Wile E. Coyote toward a tunnel entrance that’s just drawn on the side of a rock — and it gets stuck once they crash.

Eight years is pretty close to eternity when it comes to sell-by dates for topical humor, which might be one reason that the jokes in Larissa FastHorse‘s Broadway comedy The Thanksgiving Play fall flat as an underbaked pie.
Director Rachel Chavkin and her cast of gifted comic actors have layered FastHorse's already funny script with brilliant physical business.
In the real world, theatregoers will be thankful for MacArthur Genius Larissa FastHorse’s having exploded and explored the Thanksgiving story through satire both broad and subtle.
The Thanksgiving Play is genius in how it turns on itself and has stood upon the very structures that oppressed it to find its wide success.
All that work has allowed playwright Larissa FastHorse to refine her blistering satire of well-meaning white people to a sharp edge.
The play still delivers plenty of uproarious moments and this starrier Broadway cast milks them for all their worth.
It's a brilliant comedic premise that has aged like a fine wine since its 2018 off-Broadway debut at Playwrights Horizons.
FastHorse's exploration of it is for everyone's benefit, striking the balance between educational and entertaining without hammering home the reminder.
The Thanksgiving Play is a satire that entertains while it makes some very real and needed points about political correctness when dealing with unpleasant American history.
But without a distinct point of view, its bottom line of “Thanksgiving is problematic” renders it only a pleasant, toothless, pilgrimage to the theatre.
In the climate of now, these jokes are just adding to a depressingly destructive chorus.
Perhaps FastHorse should make a run for 30 Rock and leave Broadway behind.
Seen in 2023, it seems...so five years ago.
Unfortunately, the narrative drive runs out of “The Thanksgiving Play” long before Hernandez’s set attempts to stage an 11 o’clock rescue.
But how comic is it, from start to finish?

The Thanksgiving Play is both a hilarious comedy and an effective satire, a crystal clear portrait of the excesses, hypocrisies, mental gymnastics, and sometimes emptiness of so-called wokeness, particularly within the (experimental) theater community.

Her critique of well-meaning Americans is scathing, as she reminds her audience that political and social extremes are dangerous, and, on both sides, come with high levels of misunderstanding, hurtful actions, and a false sense of righteousness.
Although some in the audience found it funny, it struck me as inane.

Unfortunately, the play itself only fitfully matches the impact of these segments, often settling instead for satirizing of white liberals—which generates plenty of laughs, but sometimes feels sitcom-safe.

cn.t: FastHorse's satire of performative wokeness earns laughs but divides critics, with some finding it sharp and timely while others feel it's dated since 2015. The comedy about white liberals planning a Native American Thanksgiving play lands unevenly.

sg.ra: Multiple guides converge on Rows B to H center as the best views in Broadway's smallest house (597 seats), where the intimate scale means these seats feel closer to the stage than premium orchestra in any other Broadway theater. The Hayes-specific tradeoff: patrons repeatedly flag that the stage sits unusually high for such an intimate room, so Row A and the very front can force neck-craning — one AVFMS viewer described the Hayes stage as 'particularly high for the first couple of rows, so you'll be using your neck to look up,' and a JOB patron noted 'The stage is high so you don't see actors' feet.' Rows B-H sit far enough back to clear that stage-height issue while still letting you read facial expressions in a house this small.

sg.vl: Value sweet spot where the rake kicks in
sg.ra: Rows F-M center are consistently flagged as the value band at Hayes — priced below premium but still close in a 597-seat room. The Hayes-specific reason to favor the back half of that band (J-M) over F-I: an AVFMS reviewer explicitly observed that 'Row J in the orchestra level is where the rake of the floor starts to increase so even a short guy like me can see over someone tall.' That makes J-M the first rows where a tall head in front stops being a problem, which matters more at Hayes than at larger houses because the orchestra is 'more long than it is wide' (NYTix) and the stage height is tall, so front-orchestra sightlines are flatter than usual.

The very back row of the Hayes mezzanine sits directly against the theater's staff/operations area — a quirk specific to this post-2018-renovation layout. Multiple AVFMS reviewers independently complain the ushers or crew are audible throughout the show from Mezz Row J: one wrote 'this row butts up against the row where the theater staff sits and they chatted, loudly, throughout the show'; another said 'the ushers downstairs were loud and I could sometimes hear their murmurings'; an accessible-seat user at Mezz J-101 reported 'there's some sort of operation booth to the right of this seat and it's very loud and distracting. I could hear talking and typing throughout the entire show.' Because Hayes is the smallest house on Broadway, there's no orchestra noise to mask ambient staff chatter the way a 1,500-seat venue would — in this intimate room, the booth chatter carries.
